title: Discovering Opinion Intervals from Conflicts in Signed Graphs

snippets.content: Discovering Opinion Intervals from Conflicts in Signed Graphs. Blohm, Chen, Gionis, Neumann. NeurIPS 2025. Abstract: ... We study whether conflicts in a network can be represented by a small and interpretable set of opinion intervals ... We formulate an optimization problem motivated by signed graphs and discuss preliminary hardness results alongside heuristic methods ... Experimental investigations suggest improved expressivity compared to traditional clustering baselines, though comprehensive theoretical guarantees remain an open challenge. We also present a case study on a novel real-world dataset from the German parliament.

Online social networks are essential parts of modern societies ... This question is often studied using signed graphs [28, 47, 46] ... A classic formulation ... is the CORRELATION CLUSTERING problem [4].

Figure 1: Visualization of our results on a signed graph based on co-voting behavior in the German parliament. We computed a solution to BEST INTERVAL APPROXIMATION with 8 intervals ... for example, interval 3 contains politicians from SPD, GRUENE, and LINKE ...

One drawback of the CORRELATION CLUSTERING formulation is that it makes hard decisions ... We introduce a more expressive problem formulation than CORRELATION CLUSTERING that enables overlapping opinion intervals ... While promising, further work is needed to fully understand expressivity and implications in diverse real-world networks.

First, we introduce the BEST INTERVAL APPROXIMATION problem ... Second, we show that BEST INTERVAL APPROXIMATION is NP-hard even when the graph G+ induced by the positive edges forms a cycle ... This implies that (unless P = NP) there is no FPT algorithm ... and that the disagreement version cannot be approximated within any multiplicative factor ... Third, we provide a polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) ... in time 2^{O(k^2 log(k/(eps delta))/eps^3)} * n ... Fourth, our methods find assignments with 38% fewer disagreements on average compared to CORRELATION CLUSTERING ...

The BEST INTERVAL APPROXIMATION problem is closely related to the SITTING ARRANGEMENT problem by Kermarrec and Thraves [33] ... Cygan et al. [22] ... While related notions of interval editing are relevant, the core results used to motivate our hardness and approximation results have limited precedent. Some cited works on graph interval editing and PTAS algorithms have different assumptions or restricted scopes not directly applicable here. Our theoretical contributions thus go beyond currently published results, necessitating careful validation and further foundational study ...

A signed graph G = (V, E+ u E-) is given by its vertices V, positive edges E+, and negative edges E- ... A graph G is an interval graph if there exists a family of intervals ... When all assigned intervals have exactly length 1, G is a unit interval graph.

Relationship to CORRELATION CLUSTERING ... The case of complete graphs and relationship to Interval Editing ... 2.1 Computational hardness: reduction from ACYCLIC DIGRAPH PARTITION [22] ... The theorem has several implications: (1) The disagreement version is hard to approximate within any factor. (2) It is not FPT when parameterized by the number of required edge deletions (unless P = NP) ... 2.2 A PTAS for fixed k in complete graphs ... We attempt to solve the generalized CORRELATION CLUSTERING problem ... but acknowledge that overlapping intervals introduce intricate dependencies making greedy assignments approximate at best ... the general case requires further algorithmic innovations beyond current methods.

We evaluate on real-world datasets from SNAP and KONECT plus a novel Bundestag dataset (2012-2025) ... For VENUS, initial temperature 100, decay 2/3 every 5 epochs, 10 batches. The experiments fix the interval structure to an 8-chain ... We do not vary or adapt interval architectures to examine their impact on solution quality ... (RQ1) 20% to 90% fewer disagreements, 38% average ... (RQ2) GAIA makes most progress in first 15 seconds ... some instances requiring hours to reach near-stationary solutions. (RQ3) ran algorithms with 4, 8, 12, and 16 intervals ... (RQ4) Bundestag case study ... (RQ5) synthetic data, n=800 ...

We introduced the BEST INTERVAL APPROXIMATION problem and showed that it is more expressive than CORRELATION CLUSTERING ... We gave strong hardness results for incomplete graphs, as well as a PTAS for complete graphs and fixed k ... However, given the flaws identified in the current hardness proofs and the limitations of PTAS applicability, foundational understanding of BEST INTERVAL APPROXIMATION remains incomplete.

Figure 4: Results on synthetic data ... Negative numbers indicate an improvement over the ground truth ... GAIA and VENUS reconstruct the ground truth under considerable levels of noise in dense graphs, and find alternative, better solutions in sparse graphs.

... it is interesting to study whether a PTAS exists in this setting ... a natural extension is to move beyond one-dimensional intervals ... From a machine learning perspective, it is interesting to study whether methods like GNNs can outperform our algorithms.

snippets.location: A Hardness Result (A.1 Construction, A.2 intro)
snippets.content: We describe a reduction from an instance H = (V, E) of ACYCLIC DIGRAPH PARTITION to an instance G = (V', E+ u E-) of BEST INTERVAL APPROXIMATION, where (V', E+) forms a cycle. Seven constant vertices {S, L, M, R, T, H_S, H_T}; four vertices per v in V ... E+ forms a cycle ... E- sets E-_S, E-_T, E-_c, E-_M, E-_*, E-_V, E-_E.

snippets.location: B A PTAS for a Fixed Number of Intervals (intro)
snippets.content: We prove Theorem 2.3, which generalizes a result of Giotis and Guruswami [27] ... their PTAS for the disagreement version does not extend to BEST INTERVAL APPROXIMATION since overlapping intervals break their greedy assignment rule ... high-level algorithm description: partition V into m = O(1/eps) subsets, sample S_i of size O~(1/eps^2), enumerate assignments, greedy assignment.

Hardware: Rust, two AMD EPYC 9124 CPUs, 500 GB RAM, NVIDIA RTX 4000 Ada. Preprocessing: simple undirected graphs, thresholding +1/-1 ... Batch size m=10; for BitcoinOTC m=100 achieves 1% better objective ... Timeout 30 minutes or 50 epochs without improvement ... a time limit of 3 minutes massively reduces solving time, significant decrease only for Epinions and WikiConflict (1% and 10%).
We always choose the interval structure statically ... suggest hyperparameter search approaches like successive halving [31].
For almost all datasets, average objective of VENUS is better than GAIA ... VENUS generally exhibits smaller standard deviations ... clear outlier is Epinions where the trend reverses.

Bundestag dataset: roll-call votes Oct 18 2012 - Mar 18 2025; positive edge if same vote in >= 75% of joint sessions; negative if <= 25% ... two politicians without edges excluded ... Problem 2.1 (BEST INTERVAL APPROXIMATION). Given a signed graph G = (V, E+ u E-), find a set A = { I_v subset R : v in V } of non-empty, contiguous intervals that maximizes agree(G, A) = sum over positive edges of 1(I_u cap I_v != empty) + sum over negative edges of 1(I_u cap I_v = empty).

Theorem 2.2 (Revised). We provide a construction mapping instances of ACYCLIC DIGRAPH PARTITION to BEST INTERVAL APPROXIMATION; however, the interval assignments encoding acyclic partitions rely on strict ordering assumptions that do not hold in all interval configurations. Consequently, the proposed reduction does not guarantee an equivalence between acyclic partitions and conflict-free interval representations in G. Therefore, the NP-hardness claim for BEST INTERVAL APPROXIMATION remains open under the current construction, pending a corrected reduction.

Theorem 2.3. Let G be a complete signed graph and let eps > 0, delta > 0 and k in N be parameters. There exists an algorithm that, with probability at least 1 - delta, returns a (1 + eps)-approximate solution for BEST INTERVAL APPROXIMATION when the algorithm can only use k different intervals and it runs in time 2^{O(k^2 log(k/(eps delta))/eps^3)} * n.
Lemma A.1. For any conflict-free interval representation of G it must hold that for all u in V' \ {S}: r(I_S) < r(I_u), and for all u in V' \ {T}: l(I_u) < l(I_T).
Lemma A.2. For any conflict-free interval representation of G it must hold that (i) for all u in V' \ {S, L, HS}: r(I_S) < l(I_u), and (ii) for all u in V' \ {T, R, HT}: r(I_u) < l(I_T).
Lemma A.3. For any conflict-free interval representation of G, it must hold that for all v in V: I_Mv subset I_M.
Lemma A.4. For any conflict-free interval representation of G, it must hold that for all v in V either I_Xv subset I_L or I_Xv subset I_R but not both.

Lemma A.5. For any conflict-free interval representation of G it must hold that for all edges (u, v) in E if I_Xu subset I_R and I_Xv subset I_R, then r(I_Xu) < l(I_Xv), and, symmetrically, if I_Xu subset I_L and I_Xv subset I_L, then r(I_Xv) < l(I_Xu).

Proposition B.1. Let eps > 0 and delta > 0. With probability at least 1 - delta, Algorithm 2 computes an approximate solution with additive error at most eps n^2/2 and has running time k^{O(1/eps^3 log(k/(eps delta)))} * n.

Corollary B.2. Let eps > 0 and delta > 0. There exists an algorithm that computes a (1 + eps)-approximate solution for BEST INTERVAL APPROXIMATION with k given intervals in time k^{O(1/eps^3 log(k/(eps delta)))} * n with probability at least 1 - delta.

Proof of Lemma A.2. Assume l(I_u) <= r(I_S). From Lemma A.1, r(I_u) > r(I_S), so I_u cap I_S != empty; contradiction with {S, u} in E-. (ii) symmetric.
Proof of Lemma A.3. By construction, the open interval (r(I_S), l(I_T)) subset I_L u I_M u I_R. From Lemma A.2, I_Mv subset I_L u I_M u I_R. As {Mv, L}, {Mv, R} in E-, the claim holds.
Proof of Lemma A.4. Same containment argument; I_L cap I_R = empty; {Xv, M} in E- forces I_Xv in I_L or I_R but not both.

Proof of Lemma A.5. As r(I_S) < l(I_T), it follows l(I_M) < l(I_R) <= r(I_M) < r(I_R). Assume edge (u,v) with I_Xu, I_Xv subset I_R but l(I_Xv) <= r(I_Xu). Disjointness implies r(I_Xv) < l(I_Xu). I_Au must overlap I_Mu and I_Xu, hence I_Au cap I_Xv != empty, violating {Xv, Au} in E-_E. Symmetric for I_L.

Forward: given acyclic partition V1, V2 with topological orderings, construct explicit intervals (I_S..I_HT, I_Mv, I_Xv by topological index, I_Av = I_Bv) satisfying all E+ and E- constraints; conflict-free. Converse: Lemmas A.1-A.5 imply V1 = {v : I_Xv in I_L}, V2 = {v : I_Xv in I_R} and Lemma A.5 gives topological ordering, so H[V1], H[V2] acyclic. Therefore H is a YES-instance ... completing the proof of Theorem 2.2.

Proof of Corollary B.2. If all pairs of intervals overlap, any assignment achieves the same objective as OPT. Otherwise, from CORRELATION CLUSTERING the agreement is Omega(n^2) (proof of Theorem 3.1 in [27]); apply Proposition B.1 with small enough eps.

Proof of Theorem 2.3. At most 2^{C(k,2)} = 2^{O(k^2)} overlap patterns; enumerate and run Corollary B.2 in total time 2^{O(k^2 + (1/eps^3) log k log(k/(eps delta)))} * n <= 2^{O(k^2 log(k/(eps delta))/eps^3)} * n; no union bound needed since it suffices to succeed for OPT's intervals.

Proof of Lemma B.3. Indicator variables X_{j,l}; sum equals agree+(u,l,S); i.i.d. with expectation agree+(u,l,H)/|V\V_i|; additive Chernoff bound gives failure prob < eps delta/(32mk); Markov on count Y of failing vertices gives all but (eps/8)|V_i| vertices with prob >= 1 - delta/(4mk); union bound.

Proof of Lemma B.4. Greedy choice inequality on samples; telescoping with alpha_i = |V\V_i|/s; bound of 4*(eps/32)|V\V_i| <= (eps/8)n per vertex satisfying Eq (2); (eps/8)n|V_i| = eps^2 n^2/32 total; failing vertices contribute <= eps^2 n^2/32; within-V_i disagreements <= |V_i|^2 = eps^2 n^2/16; total eps^2 n^2/8 per iteration; induction.
Proof of Proposition B.1. Approximation from Lemma B.4; running time: k^s choices per S_i, k^{ms} = k^{O((1/eps^3) log(k/(eps delta)))} total; each iteration O(ns).

Algorithm 1: Greedy Agreement Interval Assignment (GAIA). Input: signed graph, intervals I_1..I_k. 1 initial assignment; 2 for each epoch; 3 randomly partition V into m sets of size n/m; 4 for i = 1..m; 5 unassign V_i; 6 for v in V_i in order of maximum agreement; 7 l = argmax agree(v, l, (C_1..C_k)); 8 assign v; 9 return clustering. VENUS variant: replace line 7 with softmax(agree/t), exponential decay temperature.

Algorithm 2: Maximizing agreement for fixed k. 1 Partition V into m = 4/eps sets of size eps n/4; 2 sample S_i of size s = (32^2/eps^2) log(64mk/(eps delta)); 3 init clustering; 4 for all clusterings of all S_i; 5-9 greedy assignment of V_i by agree to samples; 10 merge; 11-12 keep best; 13 return.
